# Semantic and Feature Branches

Also called: Feature Fields, Distilled Feature Fields, Semantic NeRF branches, Opacity Fields for Detection

## Overview
Semantic and Feature Branches extend the [standard NeRF](#979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md) formulation by predicting arbitrary per-point feature signals $\mathbf{f}$ in addition to density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$ [S1]. This allows the radiance field to encode semantic labels, physical properties, or latent descriptors from foundation models, enabling tasks such as zero-shot segmentation, [object manipulation](#22032-object-manipulation.md), and 3D detection [S1, S2, S3, S4]. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific applications like pose estimation [PI-NeRF](12124-pi-nerf.md) or gaze redirection [GazeNeRF](12127-gazenerf.md), this family provides the general architectural mechanism for embedding high-dimensional feature spaces into the [volumetric representation](#21847-volumetric-representation.md).

## Shared principles
The baseline [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) architecture [Parent](11313-model-architecture-modifications.md) defines a continuous volumetric scene representation $F_\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c})$ [G]. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using [standard volume rendering equations](#1165-standard-volume-rendering-equation.md) [G]. [Feature fields](#12995-feature-fields.md) extend this by modifying the output space to predict arbitrary per-point feature signals $\mathbf{f}$ alongside density and color [S1]. Supervision is achieved by reprojecting the predicted 3D features onto the 2D image plane and comparing them to corresponding 2D feature maps, mirroring the color reconstruction process [S1]. This allows encoding semantic labels, physical properties, or latent descriptors from foundation models [S1].

The [volume rendering equation](#2098-volume-rendering-equation.md) for a ray $\mathbf{r}$ with $K$ sample points is:
$$
\hat{F}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}_k \alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}_k)\delta_k) \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_k)
$$
where $\hat{T}_k = \exp(-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \sigma(\mathbf{x}_j)\delta_j)$ is the accumulated transmittance, $\alpha(\cdot)$ is the opacity function, and $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_k)$ is the feature vector at sample point $\mathbf{x}_k$ [S1].

## Subtopics

### [PI-NeRF](12124-pi-nerf.md)
[PI-NeRF](#12124-pi-nerf.md) uses a feature branch to estimate camera pose from a single image without iterative optimization. It differs from siblings like [NeRF2Points](12125-nerf2points.md) by mapping pixel features to ray representations via an Invertible Neural Network Module (INM), enabling direct pose calculation via Perspective-n-Point (PnP). Choose this method when pose initialization is unavailable or iterative optimization is too slow. See [PI-NeRF](12124-pi-nerf.md).

### [NeRF2Points](12125-nerf2points.md)
[NeRF2Points](#12125-nerf2points.md) uses feature branches to generate large-scale, geometrically consistent RGBD point clouds from street-view data. It distinguishes itself by separating road and street components to prevent "pavement collapse" and using Geometric-Aware Consistency Regularization (GAC) to reduce floaters. Choose this for large-scale outdoor street-view reconstruction. See [NeRF2Points](12125-nerf2points.md).

### [GazeNeRF](12127-gazenerf.md)
[GazeNeRF](#12127-gazenerf.md) uses two-stream feature branches to predict volumetric features for face and eye regions separately. It differs from [Semantic-NeRF](14889-semantic-nerf.md) by explicitly modeling 3D eyeball [rotation](#19376-rotation.md) via rigid rotation of eye feature maps, allowing gaze redirection while preserving identity. Choose this for 3D-aware face editing and gaze redirection. See [GazeNeRF](12127-gazenerf.md).

### Distilled Feature Field (DFF)
DFF extends NeRF by adding a feature branch outputting a 3D feature vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ to describe semantics, supervised by distilling a 2D teacher network (e.g., LSeg, DINO) via volume rendering [S1]. For a 3D coordinate $\mathbf{x}$, the network outputs density $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$, color $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d})$, and feature vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ [S1]. Apply stop-gradient to density $\sigma$ in the rendering of features $\hat{F}(\mathbf{r})$ to prevent inconsistent supervision from harming geometry reconstruction [S1]. The teacher network is a pretrained pixel-level image encoder, specifically `clip-ViT-B-32-multilingual-v1` from Hugging Face [S1]. The weight of the [feature loss](#7699-vgg-loss-for-image-patches.md) $\mathcal{L}_f$ in the [total loss function](#4177-total-loss-function.md) is $\lambda = 0.04$ [S1]. The model uses two networks for volume rendering with [coarse-and-fine hierarchical sampling](#14488-coarse-to-fine-hierarchical-sampling.md) [S1]. Unlike SemanticNeRF which outputs closed-set label probabilities, DFF outputs a continuous feature vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ to enable zero-shot segmentation with open-set text labels [S1].

### Neural Perceptual Fields (NePeRF)
NePeRF is a method that distills 2D features into a 3D feature field for zero-shot segmentation [S1]. The weight for the feature loss term, balancing it against the color loss, is $\lambda_f = 0.04$ [S1].

### Object Segmentation Component
This component generates view-consistent object masks for all views from a single user-annotated mask, using depth information and a region encoding concept [S2]. The network introduces 'area encoding' for each sampling point in the NeRF model, representing the probability that the sampling point belongs to the occluded area [S2]. It constrains the generation of correct area encoding by correctly modeling the geometry of the scene using the depth prior from the NeRF component [S2]. It obtains semantic information of whether sampling points belong to occluded areas under the guidance of the given mask [S2]. It generates view-consistent segmentation results (masks $M$) for all views [S2].

### Feature Volume Fusion
This technique combines [feature volumes](#18218-voxel-and-grid-representations.md) from different scenes or objects into a single composition without artifacts [S3]. For each voxel coordinate shared across original scenes, it selects the feature vector with the maximum L2 norm [S3]. It uses the selected feature vector to render the fused scene, achieving tight contact between objects from different scenes [S3]. The L2 norm of the feature vector correlates with the color and density information carried by each voxel [S3]. It is used to fuse feature volumes for objects from different datasets, such as combining LLFF vase/stand volumes with AXYZ human subject volumes [S3].

### Opacity Field Estimation for Detection
Opacity field models scene geometry as probability of object presence (1.0 if opaque) [S4]. It shares the G-MLP learned in the [NeRF branch](#17510-grid-guided-nerf-branch-training.md) with the detection branch [S4]. It inputs augmented volume features of 3D detection into the [shared G-MLP](#15003-shared-g-mlp.md) [S4]. It transforms density to opacity. Since ray direction and point distance are undefined in the undirected volume, it exploits uniform voxel distribution to cancel constant $\delta_t$. Compute opacity: $\alpha(\mathbf{p}) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{p}))$ [S4]. It multiplies opacity field with feature grid for 3D detection: $\alpha(\mathbf{p}) \times V_{avg}(\mathbf{p})$ [S4]. The density output from G-MLP is $\sigma(\mathbf{p}) = \text{G-MLP}(\bar{V}(\mathbf{p}), \gamma(\mathbf{p}))$, where $\mathbf{p}$ is the center position of each voxel in the detection volume, $\sigma(\mathbf{p}) \in [0, \infty]$ [S4].

### DAP-NeRF
Particle removal and resampling are performed every 2,000 training steps [S5]. Static feature grid $G_S$ and dynamic feature grid $G_D$ resolution: $160^3$ [S5]. Number of particles: 200,000 for synthetic datasets, 500,000 for real-scene datasets [S5]. Feature dimension $C$ for both particle and voxel features: 12 [S5]. Network width: 256 [S5]. Positional encoding frequency $\nu$: 10 for $(x, y, z)$, 4 for view direction $\mathbf{d}$, 8 for time $t$ [S5]. Particle removal thresholds: alpha value $\epsilon_\alpha = 0.0001$, trajectory length $\epsilon_{traj} = 0.1$ [S5]. Random resampling radius: 0.1 times the voxel length of the feature grids [S5]. Optimizer: Adam with $\beta = (0.9, 0.99)$ [S5]. Minibatch size: 4,096 rays [S5]. Learning rate for particle features: 0.005 [S5]. Learning rate for motion predictor network $\phi_m$: 0.001 [S5]. Total training iterations: 60,000 [S5]. Learning rate decay: [exponential schedule](#11839-annealing-schedules.md), final decay factor 0.1 [S5]. Loss weights from equation (15): $w_1 = 0.01$, $w_2 = 0.001$, $w_3 = 0.01$, $w_4 = 0.01$ [S5].

### Self-Conditioned NeRF (SCNeRF)
SCNeRF leverages features from a pretrained VGG network to guide radiance field training in sparse-view settings, using two modifications: local feature descriptor constraints and explicit feature-conditioned color prediction [S6]. Modification 1: Extract feature maps $F_{gt}$ from sparse input images using a pretrained VGG model (trained on ImageNet) [S6]. For a 3D point $\mathbf{p}_i = (x, y, z)$, predict a bottleneck feature $\mathbf{b}_i$ using network $M_b$: $\mathbf{b}_i = M_b(\mathbf{p}_i)$ [S6]. Predict a prior feature $\mathbf{f}_i$ for the 3D point based on the shared bottleneck feature using network $M_f$: $\mathbf{f}_i = M_f(\mathbf{b}_i)$ [S6]. Obtain rendered feature $F(\mathbf{r})$ by volume rendering and minimize L2 loss between rendered features and extracted features $F_{gt}(\mathbf{r})$: $\mathcal{L}_f = || F(\mathbf{r}) - F_{gt}(\mathbf{r}) ||_2$ [S6]. Modification 2: Explicitly constrain the relation between feature descriptors and color predictions by conditioning the [color prediction network](#18460-appearance-implicit-neural-representations.md) on the learned prior feature $\mathbf{f}_i$ [S6]. The pretrained network is VGG trained on ImageNet [S6]. Unlike [DietNerf](#22404-dietnerf.md) which constrains learning in unobserved views with image-level loss, this method supervises the learning process in training views with pixel-level loss [S6].

### Invertible Neural Module (INM)
INM is a bidirectional converter between ray features/representations and pixel features, consisting of two INNs (INN1 and INN2) [S7]. [Ray Representation](#19057-ray-representation.md) Construction: Convert ray $\mathbf{r}_u$ to Plücker coordinates $\mathbf{r}_{plu} = [\mathbf{d}_u, \mathbf{m}_u] \in \mathbb{R}^6$ where $\mathbf{m}_u = \mathbf{o}_u \times \mathbf{d}_u$ [S7]. Calculate endpoint $\mathbf{e}_u = \mathbf{r}_u(\sigma_r)$ [S7]. Define representation $\mathbf{r}_u = [\mathbf{r}_{plu}, \mathbf{e}_u, \mathbf{e}_u]$ [S7]. Forward Path: Input ray feature $\mathbf{f}_{r_u}$ and ray representation $\mathbf{r}_u$ [S7]. Encode ray via INN1: $\mathbf{r}' = \text{INN1}(\mathbf{r}_u)$ [S7]. Output pixel feature $\mathbf{f}_u$ (implied mapping from $\mathbf{f}_{r_u}$ and $\mathbf{r}'$) [S7]. Reverse Path: Input pixel feature $\mathbf{f}_u$ [S7]. Decode via INN2 inverse: $[\mathbf{r}'', \mathbf{f}_{r''}] = \text{INN2}^{-1}(\mathbf{f}_u)$ [S7]. Decode ray via INN1 inverse: $\mathbf{r}'' = \text{INN1}^{-1}(\mathbf{r}'')$ [S7]. Output ray representation $\mathbf{r}''_u$ and ray feature $\mathbf{f}_{r''_u}$ [S7]. INN1 is used to encode the ray, with sub-networks being MLPs [S7]. INN2 consists of 3 invertible blocks, each sub-network is an MLP [S7].

### NeRF-SOS
Generate feature tensors from color patches rendered by the model using a self-supervised pretrained framework [S8]. Use the generated features to create volumes for appearance-segmentation [S8]. Apply contrastive losses to correlate appearance-segmentation and geometry-segmentation [S8].

### Feature-Realistic Fusion
Fuse general features learned from EfficientNet into the NeRF representation [S8]. Operate incrementally in real-time using a SLAM backend to manage exploration of new, unobserved scene regions [S8].

## Background
The concept of feature fields originated from the need to extend NeRF beyond color rendering to support semantic understanding and editing. [Distilled Feature Fields](#12026-distilled-feature-fields.md) (DFF) introduced the idea of distilling 2D teacher networks (like CLIP or DINO) into 3D feature fields for zero-shot segmentation [S1]. Subsequent works adapted this for specific domains: PI-NeRF for pose estimation [S7], NeRF2Points for large-scale street view geometry [S1], and GazeNeRF for facial editing [S1]. Other variants include opacity fields for 3D detection [S4], feature volume fusion for [scene manipulation](#17595-scene-editing.md) [S3], and self-conditioned features for sparse-view rendering [S6].
